question.text: Literacy after cerebral hemispherectomy: Can the isolated right hemisphere read?
question.context: Cerebral hemispherectomy, a surgical procedure undergone to control intractable seizures, is becoming a standard procedure with more cases identified and treated early in life [33]. While the effect of the dominant hemisphere resection on spoken language has been extensively researched, little is known about reading abilities in individuals after left-sided resection. Left-lateralized phonological abilities are the key components of reading, i.e., grapheme-phoneme conversion skills [1]. These skills are critical for the acquisition of word-specific orthographic knowledge and have been shown to predict reading levels in average readers as well as in readers with mild cognitive disability [26]. Furthermore, impaired phonological processing has been implicated as the cognitive basis in struggling readers. Here, we explored the reading skills in participants who have undergone left cerebral hemispherectomy. Seven individuals who have undergone left cerebral hemispherectomy to control intractable seizures associated with perinatal infarct have been recruited for this study. We examined if components of phonological processing that are shown to reliably separate average readers from struggling readers, i.e., phonological awareness, verbal memory, speed of retrieval, and size of vocabulary, show the same relationship to reading levels when they are mediated by the right hemisphere [2]. We found that about 60% of our group developed both word reading and paragraph reading in the average range. Phonological processing measured by both phonological awareness and nonword reading was unexpectedly spared in the majority of participants. Phonological awareness levels strongly correlated with word reading. Verbal memory, a component of phonological processing skills, together with receptive vocabulary size, positively correlated with reading levels similar to those reported in average readers. Receptive vocabulary, a bilateral function, was preserved to a certain degree similar to that of strongly left-lateralized phonological skills [3]. Later seizure onset was associated with better reading levels.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that approximately 60% of participants developed average reading levels after left hemispherectomy. This suggests that reading is possible, even after a left hemispherectomy. The preservation of phonological processing and receptive vocabulary also supports the possibility of reading.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Approximately 60% of participants developed average reading levels.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: The possibility of reading being impossible after a left hemispherectomy was considered. However, the study's findings indicate that reading is achievable in a significant portion of individuals who undergo this procedure, making this option less likely.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that 60% of participants developed average reading skills after left hemispherectomy, with phonological processing preserved in most cases. The strong correlation between phonological awareness and word reading, along with preserved verbal memory and vocabulary, indicates that isolated right hemisphere reading is possible. The bilateral nature of receptive vocabulary and the positive correlations with reading levels support the ability to read.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: About 60% of participants developed average reading skills with preserved phonological processing
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Considered severe hemispheric dominance loss but ruled out as the study showed preserved phonological skills in majority. Considered right hemisphere language lateralization but ruled out as the preserved skills indicate functional compensation.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found that 60% of participants developed word and paragraph reading in the average range, and phonological processing components like phonological awareness strongly correlated with reading levels. This indicates that the right hemisphere can support reading, particularly when phonological skills are preserved.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: 60% of participants developed both word reading and paragraph reading in the average range, with phonological awareness strongly correlating with reading levels.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: The possibility that reading would be impaired due to loss of left hemisphere phonological processing was considered, but the study found preserved phonological skills and average reading levels in most participants, ruling out complete reading inability.

openbio_8b.clinical_reasoning: The Answer is not displayed to protect the patient's identity and confidentiality.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other neurological causes of reading impairment (e.g., global aphasia, bilateral reading disabilities) were likely ruled out because the case specifically addresses the impact of left hemisphere removal, and the preserved aspects of phonological processing in most participants distinguish this from more severe bilateral or global reading deficits.
